anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or un-bounded growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine heaps drives the database process beyond the safe physical or virtual memory envelope. 
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: Commit processing is throttled because log buffering, flushing, segment switching, or archiving cannot keep pace with the rate of redo generation. 
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas falls to zero or below auto-extend thresholds, causing allocation failures and write stalls.

When these three root causes arise together, the instance exhibits a compound failure pattern: commit latencies and log-flush waits lengthen while overall memory consumption surges and physical free space dwindles. Checkpoints and log switches fire in rapid succession, yet archived-log backlogs and full destinations prevent reuse, so active log files balloon until the underlying volume is exhausted. As space tightens, the engine is forced to retain extra dirty buffers in memory because checkpoints cannot persist pages, amplifying memory pressure, paging, and OOM risks. Concurrently, background archiver and cleanup processes contend for both memory and I/O, further delaying log rotation and consuming the last bytes of available space. Application sessions observe timeouts, "cannot allocate extent / no space left on device" errors, and eventual instance or node eviction when the operating system can no longer satisfy memory or disk requests.

Causally, aggressive memory allocation (e.g., un-capped per-query work areas or plan-cache bloat) increases the rate and size of redo records as large in-memory operations generate heavy transactional metadata. The swollen redo stream pushes the transaction-log subsystem past its flush and switch capacity; because archives are slow or space-constrained, log segments cannot be recycled, causing on-disk log growth that quickly consumes the same storage pool where data and temp files reside. As the device fills, checkpoints stall, forcing dirty pages to remain resident and inflating memory use even further. The positive feedback loop—memory bloat → higher redo volume → log bottleneck → storage exhaustion → blocked checkpoints → more memory bloat—drives the system into a state where neither memory, log throughput, nor space can recover without external intervention.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
